clue.text: I arrest you in the name of the law

definitions.text: I arrest you in the name of the law

parts.words: I arrest you in the name of the law
parts.note: the stock line every stage or screen policeman says when collaring a suspect, so the whole clue is an example of a familiar saying

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is not an instruction but a quotation: the line is so worn that it has become the officer's trademark saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock phrase repeated so often it is tied to one speaker or role is exactly what the term names.

clue.text: Walk this side found by the lake in Cumbria

indicators.note: this points at the answer itself: the answer with the word side after it makes the Cumbrian place, so side is taken off that place name

parts.words: found by the lake in Cumbria
parts.note: Ambleside is a town at the head of Windermere in the Lake District, Cumbria
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rambler is directed to a path beside a Lake District lake.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'this' plus 'side' as one word: the answer followed by SIDE gives AMBLESIDE, a Lake District town at the head of Windermere in north-west England. Remove SIDE and the walk is left.
explanation.definitionFit: To stroll at a leisurely pace is a gentle kind of walk.

clue.text: Passage had many a study before reaching south Africa

indicators.note: the earlier pieces come first in the answer and then arrive at the last piece, so they sit before it

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword stand-in for many
a den is a private room for work, a study
ZA is the international abbreviation for South Africa, from Zuid-Afrika

explanation.surface: A traveller's passage involved a lot of study before arriving in South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passage' suggests a voyage, but it is a passage of music.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadenza is a virtuoso solo section in a concerto, a musical passage for the soloist.

clue.text: A pierrot performing in the city

indicators.note: the letters of the clown's name put on a show and so are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A French clown is putting on a show in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'performing' rearranges the letters of A PIERROT; PRETORIA is the administrative capital of South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretoria is the executive capital of South Africa, a large city.

clue.text: Smart man

parts.note: the idiom smart ... names a know-all, so the man who is smart is the one in that phrase

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Smart' as the first word of a set phrase about a know-all: the man is the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a cocky know-all is a smart alec, so the name attached to smart is this one.

clue.text: European firm, record company, it displays environmental credentials

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm
a record label is the company that issues recordings

explanation.surface: A Continental business and a music label show off their green credentials.
explanation.definitionFit: An eco label is a mark on a product certifying it meets environmental standards.

clue.text: I'm sincere arranging to take trip down memory lane

indicators.note: putting the letters in order anew, so the words before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone insists they are sincere about wanting to look back on old times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranging' rearranges the letters of I'M SINCERE.
explanation.definitionFit: To reminisce is to recall past experiences fondly, a nostalgic journey through memory.

clue.text: Stationed in new place to which one is going

definitions.text: place to which one is going

indicators.note: the letters are given a new form, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A soldier is posted to a new location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges the letters of STATIONED plus IN; 'in' looks like a link word but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A destination is the end point of a journey, where a traveller is headed.

clue.text: Town band was heard

indicators.note: something heard is spoken aloud, so the word for band is said rather than written

parts.note: a crew is a group or band of people working together

explanation.surface: A town's musical band could be heard playing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' suggests musicians but means a group of people, a crew. CREWE is a railway town in Cheshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Crewe is a town in Cheshire famous as a railway junction.

clue.text: One time going round rose-garden that is to say in compliance

indicators.note: the outer word encircles the others, placing them inside it

parts.note: once means at one time, on one occasion
a rose bed is a flower bed for roses, so a bed
IE is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is to say

explanation.surface: A gardener once tended a rose bed, which is to say they were dutiful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rose-garden' suggests flowers, but a rose bed is simply a bed. 'going round' splits the outer word after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Obedience is the act of obeying, doing as one is told: compliance with orders.

clue.text: Musician in prison?

parts.note: a prisoner occupies a cell, so a musician playing a stringed instrument is jokily one who is in a cell

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a pun: a player of the large bowed string instrument sounds like someone who lives in a cell.
explanation.definitionFit: A player of the cello is a stringed-instrument musician, whose title splits as cell plus a suffix.

clue.text: One who is tall and thin in the garden

definitions.text: One who is tall and thin in the garden

parts.words: One who is tall and thin in the garden
parts.note: a lanky person is nicknamed after the tall thin stake gardeners use to support climbing beans

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a lanky person in a garden, but the answer is both the nickname for such a person and the garden stake itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall stake supporting runner beans, and by extension a lanky person, is called this.

clue.text: Librarian's accounts?

parts.note: accounts kept by a librarian read jokily as the minding of volumes on shelves

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: the word for keeping accounts is read literally as looking after books, as a librarian does.
explanation.definitionFit: Recording a business's financial transactions is the accountancy task, literally the keeping of books.

clue.text: A beetle found underneath old French coin in the country

indicators.note: in a down answer the pieces named first sit below the coin, so they follow it

parts.note: the ecu was an old French coin
a dor is a dung beetle, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: An insect is discovered beneath an antique French coin somewhere abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'found underneath' means the A and the beetle come after the coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecuador is a South American nation on the equator.

clue.text: About with hesitant fellow from the mountains

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for circa, Latin for about
um is the sound of someone hesitating
Brian is a man's name, a fellow

explanation.surface: A hesitant man comes down from the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cumbrian Mountains are in the Lake District of north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Cumbrian describes something belonging to the Cumbrian Mountains of the Lake District.

clue.text: Cilla, feeling better after seeing gold whale!

indicators.note: the trimmed name comes after the gold, so it sits second in the answer

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold

indicators.note: someone feeling better is no longer ill, so the word Cilla loses its ill

explanation.surface: A singer recovering from illness is thrilled to spot a golden whale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feeling better' takes ILL out of CILLA, leaving CA. Cilla Black was a British singer and TV presenter.
explanation.definitionFit: The orca, or killer whale, is the largest member of the dolphin family, a toothed whale.

clue.text: How surgeons work together?

parts.note: surgeons operate, so surgeons working jointly ..., with the hyphenated spelling split as co plus a medical verb

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a pun on surgical operating done jointly.
explanation.definitionFit: To cooperate is to act jointly towards a shared aim, collaborating.

clue.text: Shady hold-up

parts.note: reads as a crooked robbery, but means something held up to give shade

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shady hold-up' sounds like a dodgy robbery; it is a sunshade that is literally held up.
explanation.definitionFit: A light umbrella carried to keep off the sun is something held aloft to make shade.

clue.text: People he embarrassed using small aperture

indicators.note: the words are thrown into confusion, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone embarrassed is caught spying through a tiny opening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embarrassed' rearranges the letters of PEOPLE HE.
explanation.definitionFit: A peephole is a small hole for looking through, as in a door.

clue.text: Not always lit intermittently

definitions.meaning: a lamp that is sometimes switched one way and sometimes the other
now and then, at irregular intervals

explanation.surface: A light flickers on and off from time to time.
explanation.definitionFit: A flickering bulb is sometimes dark, sometimes lit, while the phrase also means occasionally, from time to time.

clue.text: Last month's backing one had for money in Africa

indicators.note: going backwards, so the month abbreviation is read in reverse

parts.note: December is the last month of the year, abbreviated Dec
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Last month someone was paid in African currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns DEC into CED. The cedi is the currency of Ghana.
explanation.definitionFit: The cedi is the monetary unit of Ghana, a West African currency.

clue.text: I entered stronghold once in Spain

indicators.note: the letter goes into the fortress word, so it is placed inside

parts.note: a castle is a fortified stronghold

explanation.surface: I went into a fortress in old Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' marks a former kingdom: Castile was a medieval Spanish kingdom.
explanation.definitionFit: Castile was a historic kingdom of central Spain, now a region.

clue.text: Eastern journalists thus going round for coffee

indicators.note: the short word surrounds the other, so it is split with the other placed inside

parts.note: so means thus, in this way
the press is journalists collectively

explanation.surface: Reporters in the East are making the rounds for a caffeine fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going round' makes the two-letter word for thus wrap the journalists, so its letters sit on either side of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Espresso is strong black coffee made by forcing steam through ground beans.

clue.text: So daring a change seen along the way

indicators.note: a change to these letters means they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bold change of direction is noticed by travellers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges the letters of SO DARING.
explanation.definitionFit: A road sign is a notice by the roadside, seen by drivers on their route.

clue.text: Land of the living

parts.note: reads as the world of those alive, but a living is a vicar's benefice, and this is the land attached to it

explanation.walkthrough: 'The living' is not the alive but a church benefice; the answer is the land that went with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Glebe is a portion of land assigned to a parish priest as part of his benefice.

clue.text: How fish had settled?

parts.note: a perch is a fish, and to perch is to settle, so a fish verb with a past ending gives settled

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: a freshwater fish name used as a verb meaning to alight.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds that have landed and sat on a branch have alighted, which shares its spelling with a fish name plus ed.

clue.text: Tube avoided, say

indicators.note: say signals the word is spoken, so the synonym is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to duck is to dodge, so avoided means ducked

explanation.surface: Someone dodged the Underground, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tube' suggests the London Underground but is a pipe or channel.
explanation.definitionFit: A duct is a tube or channel carrying air, fluid or cables.

clue.text: Rash having invaded us violently

indicators.note: the words are shaken up with force, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An itchy skin outbreak has spread over us aggressively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like a skin complaint but means reckless. 'violently' rearranges INVADED US.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting without advice or proper thought is reckless, as a hasty decision is.

clue.text: Former province of birth

definitions.meaning: relating to being born, as in prenatal

explanation.surface: Someone recalls an old province where they were born.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal was a province of South Africa until 1994, and the adjective natal means relating to birth.

clue.text: Transport charge?

parts.note: reads as a bus or train fare, but transport also means to enrapture, a sense shared with a word for a way in, and charge means fee

explanation.walkthrough: 'Transport' is a verb meaning to delight, the same as the word for a doorway; the charge is the price of admission, not a travel fare.
explanation.definitionFit: An admission fee is the cost of being let into a venue, such as a museum or club.
